chapters.title: Chapter 7: Market Making Across Asset Classes

lessons.title: How the Three-Cost Framework Changes Across Asset Classes

body.text: Spread equals order processing cost plus inventory holding cost plus adverse selection cost, on every instrument this course has covered. What actually drives each of those three terms is almost unrecognisably different once you move from a stock option to a currency future to a commodity contract.

children.text: Order Processing Cost Across Asset Classes

For a single-stock or index option, order processing cost is close to what Chapter 2 originally described: exchange fees, technology, and compliance overhead, reducible through SEBI's Liquidity Enhancement Scheme fee waivers on illiquid contracts. USDINR futures add a subtler version of the same cost: a $1,000 notional lot is small relative to typical institutional exposure sizes, so achieving a given economic position requires more contracts and more messages than an equivalent-sized equity position would, raising the relative processing and message-handling load per rupee of exposure. MCX contracts add a genuinely new category: a physically-deliverable contract approaching expiry carries real warehousing, quality-certification, and logistics overhead if it is not unwound in time, a cost with no equivalent anywhere in equity or currency derivatives.
Inventory Holding Cost Across Asset Classes

Chapters 2 and 3 tied inventory holding cost to volatility and expected time to offload. That still holds everywhere, but each asset class layers something on top of it. USDINR inventory carries the added overnight gap risk from the previous lesson, since the global dollar market keeps moving even while a market maker's book is closed for the night, effectively making every overnight position riskier than an equivalent intraday one, independent of volatility alone. A physically-deliverable MCX contract adds a hard ceiling on acceptable holding time as expiry approaches: unlike a cash-settled Nifty option, where the main cost of running inventory into expiry is price risk, a deliverable gold position left too late faces an entirely separate, operational forcing function to unwind, on top of the usual price-driven inventory cost.
Adverse Selection Cost Across Asset Classes

This is where the differences run deepest. A single-stock option's adverse selection cost, from Chapter 4, is driven by firm-specific information, and PIN and VPIN can be read fairly directly as estimates of genuine informed trading. USDINR complicates that reading: a large one-sided flow signal might be genuine macro-informed trading, or it might be RBI intervention, whose typical purpose is to dampen rather than exploit a move, so the same order flow toxicity signal needs a different interpretive lens than it does on a stock. MCX complicates it further still: the same rising VPIN reading could mean crude oil facing a genuine geopolitical supply shock, which is real informed-style risk, or it could mean gold facing predictable, calendar-driven wedding season demand, which looks identical mechanically but calls for a completely different response.

body.caption: The same three costs, three very different sets of drivers

Fees plus real warehousing and delivery logistics overhead near expiry on deliverable contracts
Driven by volatility and expected offload time
Same, plus overnight gap risk from a globally-traded underlying
Same, plus a hard forced-unwind deadline ahead of expiry on deliverable contracts
Firm-specific information; PIN and VPIN read fairly directly

body.text: The tools themselves, the three-cost decomposition, PIN, VPIN, Little's Law, generalise across every asset class this course has covered without needing new mathematics. What changes, and what actually separates a good market maker from a mediocre one across asset classes, is correctly interpreting what a given signal means in the specific context of the instrument being quoted, not simply running the same model everywhere unchanged.

body.title: Same Signal, Two Instruments
body.scenario: A market maker's VPIN reading rises sharply on two different books in the same week: once on a single-stock option two days before that company's quarterly results, and once on MCX gold two days before Dhanteras.
body.prompt: Should this market maker interpret and respond to these two VPIN spikes identically? Explain using this lesson's framework.
body.modelAnswer: No. The single-stock option's VPIN spike ahead of results should be read close to Chapter 4's original framing: rising probability of genuinely informed order flow, warranting a wider spread and tighter risk limits specifically because the direction of the coming information is unknown and could be sharply adverse. The gold VPIN spike ahead of Dhanteras is mechanically the same signal, one-sided volume imbalance, but it reflects predictable, calendar-driven physical demand rather than private information; the more useful response there is proactive inventory and risk-limit planning made well in advance, as covered in the previous lesson, rather than defensive real-time spread widening as if facing an unknown informational threat. Treating both spikes identically would either under-react to genuine informational risk in the stock, or over-react defensively to entirely foreseeable seasonal demand in gold.

body.title: What Actually Generalises
body.question: According to this lesson, what is the single biggest difference in how the three-cost spread framework applies across equity, currency, and commodity market making?
options: The framework itself must be replaced with entirely different mathematics for each asset class
The three cost components and the tools used to estimate them generalise well; what differs most is the correct real-world interpretation of what drives each component in a specific asset class
Adverse selection cost does not exist at all outside of equity options
Order processing cost is the only component that ever changes across asset classes
body.explanation: The lesson's central point is that the mechanics, the spread decomposition, PIN, VPIN, and Little's Law, carry over directly across asset classes without needing new formulas. What genuinely differs is the underlying driver behind each component, RBI intervention instead of ordinary informed trading in currencies, seasonal demand instead of informed trading in gold, physical delivery instead of pure cash settlement in commodities, all of which change how a signal should be read and acted on, not how it is calculated.

points: Order processing cost is shaped by exchange fees everywhere, but currency futures add relative message load from small lot sizes, and deliverable commodities add real warehousing and logistics overhead
Inventory holding cost is driven by volatility and offload time everywhere, but currency futures add overnight gap risk and deliverable commodities add a hard pre-expiry unwind deadline

Adverse selection cost is the component that differs most in substance: firm-specific information in equities, macro information complicated by RBI intervention risk in currencies, and a genuine split between informational shocks and predictable seasonal demand in commodities
The same tools, PIN, VPIN, and Little's Law, work mechanically the same way across all three asset classes

Correctly reading what a given signal means in its specific asset-class context, not simply running an unchanged model everywhere, is what actually separates strong market making practice across asset classes
The final lesson in this chapter puts a Bank Nifty options desk and a commodity futures desk side by side in a single case study to make this comparison concrete
